result.overall: The judicial review application is granted because the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) unreasonably interpreted and applied subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act regarding the admissibility of new evidence, specifically a 2002 school diploma, which was wrongly excluded and prejudiced the applicant's credibility assessment.

themes.name: Admissibility of new evidence
themes.summary: The decision focuses on whether the RAD reasonably interpreted and applied subsection 110(4) of the Act regarding the admissibility of new evidence not before the RPD, specifically a 2002 school diploma.

themes.name: Standard of review
themes.summary: The Court discusses the appropriate standard of review for the RAD's interpretation and application of subsection 110(4), concluding that reasonableness applies.

themes.name: Role and function of RAD vs PRRA officer
themes.summary: The decision distinguishes the RAD's appellate role from the PRRA officer's function, affecting the applicability of the Raza test for admissibility of new evidence.

themes.name: Credibility and identity findings
themes.summary: The applicant's credibility and identity were central to the refugee claim, with the 2002 diploma being critical evidence to challenge the RPD's negative findings.

themes.name: Procedural fairness and evidentiary flexibility
themes.summary: The Court emphasizes the importance of allowing a full fact-based appeal and the need for flexible admissibility criteria to ensure procedural fairness.

arguments.quote: The diploma would allegedly confirm that the RPD had unreasonably determined that the applicant failed to demonstrate his identity, and that he was not credible.
arguments.claim: The diploma would confirm that the RPD unreasonably determined that the applicant failed to demonstrate his identity and was not credible.

arguments.quote: The RAD applied the jurisprudence of this Court interpreting paragraph 113(a) of the Act mutatis mutandis to the interpretation of its subsection 110(4).
arguments.claim: The RAD applied the jurisprudence interpreting paragraph 113(a) of the Act mutatis mutandis to interpret subsection 110(4).

arguments.quote: While the RAD ultimately held that the RPD unreasonably determined that the applicant had failed to satisfactorily demonstrate his identity for other reasons, the applicant maintains that the credibility determination was compromised by the RAD’s refusal to admit his new evidence.
arguments.claim: The RAD held that the RPD unreasonably determined that the applicant failed to satisfactorily demonstrate his identity for other reasons.

arguments.quote: While the RAD ultimately held that the RPD unreasonably determined that the applicant had failed to satisfactorily demonstrate his identity for other reasons, the applicant maintains that the credibility determination was compromised by the RAD’s refusal to admit his new evidence.
arguments.claim: The credibility determination was compromised by the RAD’s refusal to admit the new evidence.

arguments.quote: II. The RPD decision [13] The applicant’s refugee claim hearing was rejected on May 1, 2013. The RPD held that the applicant failed to satisfactorily establish his identity.
arguments.claim: The RPD rejected the applicant's refugee claim on May 1, 2013, finding that he failed to satisfactorily establish his identity.

arguments.quote: However, only the grade 10 diploma was before the RPD. In addition to not confirming his identity, the fact that the 2002 diploma was missing could not corroborate that the applicant had studied with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.
arguments.claim: The RPD found that the applicant's grade 12 diploma was missing and that only the grade 10 diploma was before the RPD, which did not corroborate his claim of studying with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.

arguments.quote: The RPD did not believe that CIC was in possession of the document. Moreover, considering the importance of this evidence for the applicant’s narrative, the RPD held that his inability to produce it negatively affected his credibility.
arguments.claim: The RPD did not believe that Citizenship and Immigration Canada possessed the applicant's grade 12 diploma and held that the applicant's inability to produce it negatively affected his credibility.

arguments.quote: The RPD did not believe that the applicant’s birth certificate was sufficient to demonstrate his identity.
arguments.claim: The RPD did not believe the applicant's birth certificate was sufficient to demonstrate his identity.

arguments.quote: Despite not being satisfied with his identity demonstration, the RPD continued with its analysis, concluding that even had the applicant sufficiently demonstrated his identity, his refugee claim would still have been denied because it lacked credibility.
arguments.claim: The RPD concluded that even if the applicant had demonstrated his identity, his refugee claim lacked credibility and would have been denied.

arguments.quote: Notably, the RPD drew negative inferences from the fact that the applicant had amended his original Basis of Claim form [BOC] to reflect that his father’s stroke occurred between his two arrests (and not following his second arrest). The Board considered this to be a significant event in the applicant’s life, and so he should not have made a chronological error in this respect.
arguments.claim: The RPD drew negative inferences from the applicant's amendment of his Basis of Claim form regarding the timing of his father's stroke, considering it a significant event that should not have been chronologically misstated.

arguments.quote: The RPD also drew negative inferences as it seemingly misunderstood the difference between a heart attack and a stroke. The applicant had written in his BOC that his father had suffered a stroke, and had produced a medical report indicating that his father had suffered from facial paralysis in late November 2012, and was advised to seek bed rest for five days. Yet the RPD could not accept that a man suffering from a heart condition would be issued such a medical report. Moreover, the applicant had testified that his father became bedridden, almost paralyzed, and required assistance to complete basic life tasks; yet the medical note does not mention a bedridden person, but rather someone who suffers from facial paralysis and who has to stay in bed for a five-day period.
arguments.claim: The RPD misunderstood the difference between a heart attack and a stroke and did not accept the medical report indicating the applicant's father suffered facial paralysis and was advised bed rest, doubting the severity of the condition described.

arguments.quote: The RPD also did not believe that the applicant had to go to the hospital following the torture he suffered when first detained, as the medical note he produced (and the list of drugs it claims were administered to him) does not corroborate his allegations. No explanation was provided as to why these specific drugs would not be administered to a torture victim.
arguments.claim: The RPD did not believe the applicant needed hospital care following torture because the medical note and list of drugs did not corroborate his allegations, and no explanation was given for the absence of certain drugs.

arguments.quote: Finally, even had the applicant established his identity and been considered credible, he had an internal flight alternative [IFA] in Mumbai, Delhi or Bangalore.
arguments.claim: The RPD found that the applicant had an internal flight alternative in Mumbai, Delhi, or Bangalore, even if identity and credibility were established.

arguments.quote: The applicant appealed this decision to the RAD, invoking three main grounds: (1) the RPD erred in analyzing his identity; (2) the RPD did not properly evaluate his credibility; and (3) the RPD erred in its IFA analysis.
arguments.claim: The applicant appealed to the RAD arguing that the RPD erred in analyzing his identity, did not properly evaluate his credibility, and erred in its internal flight alternative analysis.

arguments.quote: On September 26, 2013 the applicant’s appeal was rejected by a one member panel of the RAD.
arguments.claim: The applicant's appeal was rejected by a one member panel of the RAD on September 26, 2013.

arguments.quote: III. The Impugned RAD Decision [23] The applicant sought to produce his 2002 high school diploma before the RAD, arguing that it was new evidence pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Act.
arguments.claim: The applicant sought to produce his 2002 high school diploma before the RAD as new evidence under subsection 110(4) of the Act.

arguments.quote: Pursuant to subsection 3(3) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules, SOR/2012-257, the applicant submitted a written statement detailing how his documentary evidence satisfied the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act.
arguments.claim: The applicant submitted a written statement detailing how his documentary evidence satisfied the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act.

arguments.quote: The RAD determined that subsection 110(4) is very similar to paragraph 113(a) of the Act, which deals with the admissibility of fresh evidence before a PRRA officer.
arguments.claim: The RAD determined that subsection 110(4) is very similar to paragraph 113(a) of the Act, which deals with admissibility of fresh evidence before a PRRA officer.

arguments.quote: As such, the RAD applied the criteria emanating from Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 [Raza] at para 13, and evaluated the credibility, the relevance, the newness, and the materiality of the evidence in order to decide on its admissibility.
arguments.claim: The RAD applied the criteria from Raza v Canada, evaluating credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality of the evidence to decide on its admissibility.

arguments.quote: In his written statement, the applicant pled that he only became aware on June 11, 2013 that this document had been faxed on February 25, 2013 by CIC (which had seized it on January 29, 2013) to the applicant’s former lawyer. As such, it had been impossible for him to produce it before the RPD.
arguments.claim: The applicant argued he only became aware on June 11, 2013 that the diploma had been faxed on February 25, 2013 by CIC to his former lawyer, making it impossible to produce before the RPD.

arguments.quote: The applicant argued that he needed it for his appeal in order to prove that the RPD had erred in not believing that CIC had seized it.
arguments.claim: The applicant argued he needed the diploma for his appeal to prove the RPD erred in not believing that CIC had seized it.

arguments.quote: Considering that his failure to produce this diploma negatively affected his overall credibility, the applicant argued that it was of paramount importance to have it before the RAD.
arguments.claim: The applicant argued that failure to produce the diploma negatively affected his overall credibility and it was paramount to have it before the RAD.

arguments.quote: The RAD concluded that at the date of the hearing before the RPD, the applicant could have produced the document, and so it could not be admissible before the RAD.
arguments.claim: The RAD concluded that at the date of the RPD hearing, the applicant could have produced the document, so it was not admissible before the RAD.

arguments.quote: Considering that he had not taken a complaint procedure against his former lawyer for failing to advise him that the document was in her possession before the RPD hearing, the RAD presumed that the applicant had been made aware of the document’s retrieval from CIC:
arguments.claim: The RAD presumed the applicant had been made aware of the document’s retrieval from CIC because he had not taken a complaint procedure against his former lawyer for failing to advise him.

arguments.quote: The RAD also dismissed the applicant’s request for a hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the Act, in order to reassess his credibility in light of the production of the 2002 diploma. Considering the document was deemed inadmissible, there was no ground to hold a hearing.
arguments.claim: The RAD dismissed the applicant’s request for a hearing under subsection 110(6) to reassess credibility in light of the diploma because the document was deemed inadmissible.

arguments.quote: Un membre du Barreau du Québec a envers son client, un devoir de compétence ainsi que des obligations de loyauté, d’intégrité, d’indépendance, de désintéressement, de diligence et de prudence. Dans le cadre de la présente procédure d’appel, l’appelant n’a pas invoqué que son avocate a agi avec incompétence et il n’a pas fourni la preuve qu’il avait, d’une manière ou d’une autre, formulé une plainte contre son ancienne avocate et que celle-ci en a été informée de manière à ce qu’elle puisse, au besoin, se faire entendre à ce sujet.
arguments.claim: The RAD noted that the applicant did not allege incompetence by his former lawyer nor provide proof of a complaint against her.

arguments.quote: As such, the three grounds of appeal (dealing with the applicant’s identity, his credibility, and his IFA) were reviewed on the reasonableness standard.
arguments.claim: The RAD reviewed the three grounds of appeal (identity, credibility, IFA) on the reasonableness standard.

arguments.quote: With respect to the applicant’s identity, the RAD held that the RPD unreasonably concluded that he had failed to satisfactorily demonstrate it.
arguments.claim: The RAD held that the RPD unreasonably concluded the applicant failed to satisfactorily demonstrate his identity.

arguments.quote: In doing so, the RAD noted that its purpose is not to “re-evaluate the evidence,” nor to proceed with “a microscopic analysis” of the RPD’s decision, but rather determine whether this was a reasonable outcome.
arguments.claim: The RAD stated its role is not to re-evaluate evidence or do a microscopic analysis but to determine if the outcome was reasonable.

arguments.quote: The RAD agreed that the applicant had failed to make sufficient efforts in order to provide documents establishing his identity, and that the RPD was right to draw a negative credibility finding in this respect.
arguments.claim: The RAD agreed the applicant failed to make sufficient efforts to provide identity documents and the RPD was right to draw a negative credibility finding on that.

arguments.quote: Nonetheless, it was unreasonable that the RPD did not consider the probative value of the school diploma (and the 1998 report card) in assessing whether the applicant had satisfactorily demonstrated his identity, even though it had assessed the document for other reasons.
arguments.claim: The RAD found it unreasonable that the RPD did not consider the probative value of the school diploma and 1998 report card in assessing identity, though it assessed the documents for other reasons.

arguments.quote: However, the RAD determined that the RPD’s overall credibility assessment was reasonable.
arguments.claim: The RAD determined the RPD’s overall credibility assessment was reasonable.

arguments.quote: Finally, the RAD did not address the RPD’s determination with respect to his IFA, considering the applicant was deemed not to be credible.
arguments.claim: The RAD did not address the RPD’s determination on the applicant’s IFA because the applicant was deemed not credible.

arguments.quote: The parties both plead that the RAD owes the RPD deference and that it should review the RPD decision applying the reasonableness standard. Respectfully, I do not agree.
arguments.claim: The RAD owes the RPD deference and should review the RPD decision applying the reasonableness standard.

arguments.quote: As regards the standard of review applied by this Court, the respondent argues that the RAD’s determination of the appropriate analysis that is to be conducted in assessing the admissibility of new evidence should be subject to the reasonableness standard, as it involves a tribunal considering and applying its home statute: while errors of law are generally governed by a correctness standard. “ Dunsmuir [v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9] (at para. 54), says that if the interpretation of the home statute or a closely related statute by an expert decision maker is reasonable, there is no error of law justifying intervention ” (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 44).
arguments.claim: The RAD’s determination of the appropriate analysis for assessing admissibility of new evidence should be subject to the reasonableness standard as it involves a tribunal applying its home statute, while errors of law are generally governed by a correctness standard.

arguments.quote: The respondent further cites Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission) v Whatcott, 2013 SCC 11 at para 167, interpreting Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner) v Alberta Teachers’ Association, [2011] 3 SCR 654 [Alberta Teachers] at para 30 on the exceptions where correctness will apply: This principle [of deference] applies unless the interpretation of the home statute falls into one of the categories of questions to which the correctness standard continues to apply, i.e., “constitutional questions, questions of law that are of central importance to the legal system as a whole and that are outside the adjudicator’s expertise, . . . ‘[q]uestions regarding the jurisdictional lines between two or more competing specialized tribunals’ [and] true questions of jurisdiction or vires . . . ”.
arguments.claim: The exceptions where correctness applies include constitutional questions, questions of law of central importance to the legal system as a whole and outside the adjudicator’s expertise, questions regarding jurisdictional lines between specialized tribunals, and true questions of jurisdiction or vires.

arguments.quote: As such, the respondent argues that the admissibility of new evidence before the RAD is within the tribunal’s expertise and does not involve a question of central importance to the legal system as a whole or any other special circumstances that would require review on a correctness standard.
arguments.claim: The admissibility of new evidence before the RAD is within the tribunal’s expertise and does not involve a question of central importance to the legal system or special circumstances requiring correctness review.

arguments.quote: The applicant argues that by not admitting the 2002 school diploma into evidence, the RAD failed to admit a document that not only goes to the core of his story, but also to the RPD’s finding of credibility which consequently, gravely prejudices his claim.
arguments.claim: The RAD failed to admit the 2002 school diploma into evidence, which goes to the core of his story and the RPD's finding of credibility, gravely prejudicing his claim.

arguments.quote: The RAD failed to properly apply Raza, as this “new evidence” satisfies the Raza test insofar that the document: (a) is credible; (b) is pertinent; (c) is “new” in that it can refute a factual conclusion drawn by the RPD; (d) is of substantial character; and (e) was not raised before the board through no fault of the applicant.
arguments.claim: The RAD failed to properly apply the Raza test, as the new evidence satisfied all its criteria: credibility, pertinence, newness, substantial character, and was not raised before through no fault of the applicant.

arguments.quote: The RAD could not have reasonably expected that it be produced by the applicant at the time of the RPD hearing.
arguments.claim: The RAD could not have reasonably expected the applicant to produce the document at the time of the RPD hearing.

arguments.quote: The applicant adds that the RAD failed to give sufficient weight to the following factors: 1. The document was of critical probative value to the applicant’s claim because it proved that he attended school with Bhupinder Singh at that time and that he was not lying about this fact; 2. Although the document was initially seized by the CBSA, the RPD did not believe this part of the applicant’s testimony when in fact it was true (i.e. this demonstrates that the applicant was not lying); and 3. The RAD recognized that the failure to produce the document was the fault of the lawyer yet nonetheless it blamed the applicant, whose case was entirely in the hands of his lawyer(s), and who likely did not know what documents may have been missing from his file or that the document in question was of such critical importance to his claim.
arguments.claim: The RAD failed to give sufficient weight to factors showing the document's critical probative value, the truth of the applicant's testimony about the document's seizure, and that the applicant was unfairly blamed for his lawyer's failure to produce it.

arguments.quote: Meanwhile, the respondent argues the RAD used the proper test by interpreting subsection 110(4) of the Act in light of similar wording in paragraph 113(a); an interpretation of the latter can assist this Court in interpreting the former. Accordingly, the respondent agrees that the series of factors set forth in Raza apply, and that it was available to the RAD to consider them.
arguments.claim: The RAD used the proper test by interpreting subsection 110(4) in light of paragraph 113(a), and the Raza factors apply and were available to the RAD to consider.

arguments.quote: The applicant was required to establish that he could not have reasonably been expected to provide the newly submitted documents at his RPD hearing. The respondent maintains the RAD did not err in finding that he failed to do so.
arguments.claim: The applicant was required to establish that he could not have reasonably been expected to provide the new documents at the RPD hearing, and the RAD did not err in finding he failed to do so.

arguments.quote: [59] In the case at bar, the evidence at issue could be material for demonstrating that the RPD erred in two key credibility findings: first, the RPD wrongly believed that the CBSA had not confiscated the 2002 diploma, and second, that the document lends further credence that the applicant did in fact go to school with Bhupinder Singh until 2002. These findings surely affected the totality of the credibility assessment made by the RPD.
arguments.claim: The evidence at issue could show that the RPD erred in two key credibility findings: that the CBSA had not confiscated the 2002 diploma, and that the applicant did go to school with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court accepted these points as material to credibility assessment.

arguments.quote: Moreover, it was not reasonable for the RAD to conclude that the applicant should have brought the documentary evidence before the RPD. The document was not in his possession, and he mistakenly believed that CBSA still had it, based on the fact that the agency had seized it from him initially.
arguments.claim: It was not reasonable for the RAD to conclude that the applicant should have brought the documentary evidence before the RPD because the document was not in his possession and he mistakenly believed CBSA still had it.

arguments.quote: The RAD seemingly recognized that the failure to produce the document was the fault of the lawyer. The CBSA had faxed it to the lawyer after the RPD hearing and the lawyer had failed to forward it to the applicant before the RAD determination.
arguments.claim: The failure to produce the document was the fault of the lawyer, who received it from CBSA after the RPD hearing but failed to forward it to the applicant before the RAD determination.

arguments.quote: As a result of certain comments made by the Court during the hearing, counsel for the respondent, with the consent of counsel for the applicant, subsequently proposed the same question of general importance as was proposed before Justice Phelan in Huruglica: Within the RAD’s statutory framework where the appeal proceeds on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the Refugee Protection Division, does the RAD owe deference to RPD findings of fact and of mixed fact and law?
arguments.claim: The respondent proposed a question of general importance for certification regarding whether the RAD owes deference to RPD findings of fact and of mixed fact and law under the RAD's statutory framework.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court did not accept this question as determinative.

holdings.quote: Mr. Parminder Singh seeks judicial review of a decision by the RAD, dated September 26, 2013, whereby it confirmed the decision of the RPD that he is neither a Convention refugee within the meaning of section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [Act] nor a person in need of protection under its subsection 97(1).
holdings.statement: Mr. Parminder Singh seeks judicial review of a decision by the RAD dated September 26, 2013, confirming the RPD decision that he is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

holdings.quote: In its analysis of the RPD decision, the RAD applied the reasonableness standard; it considered its mandate essentially akin to that of this Court when undertaking a judicial review of a RPD decision.
holdings.statement: The RAD applied the reasonableness standard in its analysis of the RPD decision, considering its mandate akin to that of this Court when undertaking judicial review of RPD decisions.

holdings.quote: However and as indicated above, the principal issue in this application for judicial review, as framed by the applicant, is whether it was reasonable for the RAD to refuse to admit a piece of evidence—a 2002 grade 12 diploma—that had not been before the RPD, pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Act.
holdings.statement: The principal issue is whether it was reasonable for the RAD to refuse to admit a 2002 grade 12 diploma not before the RPD, pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Act.

holdings.quote: For the reasons discussed below, this application for judicial review will be granted.
holdings.statement: This application for judicial review will be granted.

holdings.quote: During his school days, the applicant was friends with one Bhupinder Singh. He graduated in 2002, at which time he returned to his family’s farm.
holdings.statement: The applicant was friends with Bhupinder Singh during his school days and graduated in 2002 before returning to his family farm.

holdings.quote: In November 2012, after several years of not having heard from him, Bhupinder Singh showed up unannounced at the applicant’s house to spend the night. A few days later, the Indian police arrived at the applicant’s house and arrested him in order to ask him questions about Bhupinder Singh. The applicant was detained, tortured and released three days later. He was admitted to a hospital for five days, where he was treated for stomach pains.
holdings.statement: Bhupinder Singh unexpectedly visited the applicant in November 2012, after which the applicant was arrested, detained, tortured, hospitalized, and later released.

holdings.quote: The applicant was arrested a second time, 15 days later, in order to be asked more questions about Bhupinder Singh. After a 1 day detention, he was unconditionally released.
holdings.statement: The applicant was arrested a second time 15 days later, detained for one day, and then unconditionally released.

holdings.quote: Following his second arrest, the applicant’s mother decided to pay an agent so her son could safely leave India. He left India on January 28, 2013, and arrived in Canada the following day. His inland refugee claim was received on February 21, 2013.
holdings.statement: Following the second arrest, the applicant's mother paid an agent to help him leave India; he left on January 28, 2013, arrived in Canada the next day, and filed an inland refugee claim on February 21, 2013.

holdings.quote: However, the issue before the Court is rather whether the RAD erred in its interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act by using the Raza test and if it reasonably applied it.
holdings.statement: The issue before the Court is whether the RAD erred in its interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act by using the Raza test and if it reasonably applied it.

holdings.quote: I agree with the respondent.
holdings.statement: The Court agrees with the respondent that the admissibility of new evidence before the RAD is within the tribunal’s expertise and does not require correctness standard review.

holdings.quote: Therefore, I am of the view that both the RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act (as a question of law that is not of general importance to the legal system as a whole and outside the expertise of the RAD) and its application to the facts of this case (as a question of mixed fact and law) are to be reviewed on the reasonableness standard.
holdings.statement: Both the RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act and its application to the facts are to be reviewed on the reasonableness standard.

holdings.quote: It is worthwhile to explore whether it is reasonable for there to be an application of paragraph 113(a) jurisprudence when considering said paragraph mutatis mutandis to subsection 110(4) of the Act.
holdings.statement: It is worthwhile to explore whether paragraph 113(a) jurisprudence applies mutatis mutandis to subsection 110(4) of the Act.

holdings.quote: Unlike a PRRA officer, the RAD is a quasi-judicial administrative tribunal, trusted to act as an instance of appeal of the RPD’s determination of a refugee’s claim. While both a PRRA decision and a RPD decision in certain instances of restriction—as detailed in subsection 110(2), are not subject to appeal, except in circumstances where there are applications for leave and for judicial review by this Court, the RPD’s determination of a claim not falling under the scope of a restriction stipulated under subsection 110(2) is subject to an automatic right of appeal to the RAD. Only upon receiving the “final” RAD decision can the claimant seek leave to this Court. Moreover, in revisiting the RPD’s decision, unlike this Court, the RAD has the power—as expressly granted by the legislature under paragraph 111(b), to set aside the RPD’s decision and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made. A PRRA officer is not a quasi-judicial body, nor does he or she have an appellate function when faced with a RPD decision. The PRRA officer is an employee of the Minister, acting within his or her employer’s discretion (insofar as it is circumscribed by the Act and the Regulations). The PRRA officer must give deference to the RPD’s determination of the claim, to the extent that the facts remain unchanged from the time it had rendered its decision. Instead, the PRRA officer is specifically looking as to whether new evidence has come to life since the RPD’s rejection of the claim for determining a risk of persecution, a danger of torture, a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
holdings.statement: The RAD is a quasi-judicial administrative tribunal with appellate powers over the RPD's decisions, unlike a PRRA officer who lacks appellate function and must defer to the RPD's findings.

holdings.quote: The underlying rationale for paragraph 113(a) of the Act is not appellate in nature but rather to assure the claimant has a last chance to have any new risks of refoulement (not previously assessed by the RPD) assessed before removal can take place.
holdings.statement: The rationale for paragraph 113(a) is not appellate but to ensure claimants have a last chance to present new risks of refoulement before removal.

holdings.quote: The language of paragraph 113(a) is similar to that of subsection 110(4). The latter provision sets out that the RAD can only declare evidence admissible if it arose after the RPD’s rejection of the claim or if it was not reasonably available or if the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it (unlike for paragraph 113(a), the French version of subsection 110(4) does not use “reasonably have been expected” but rather the equivalent of “normally have been expected”). The RAD however considers this evidence in a very different light than does the PRRA officer; it is doing so in an appellate review of the correctness of the RPD’s determination.
holdings.statement: The language of paragraph 113(a) is similar to subsection 110(4), but the RAD considers evidence differently in its appellate review role.

holdings.quote: I recognize that an appeal to the RAD is mostly intended as a “paper-based” appeal.
holdings.statement: An appeal to the RAD is mostly a paper-based appeal.

holdings.quote: However, in considering whether to grant a hearing, the RAD may only look to admissible evidence. Given this requirement, the approach taken to applying admissibility criteria - either strictly or leniently - is of paramount importance because when a claimant, who is deserving of a hearing, is refused one, serious issues of procedural equity are potentially implicated.
holdings.statement: The RAD may only consider admissible evidence when deciding whether to grant a hearing, making the approach to admissibility criteria crucial to procedural fairness.

holdings.quote: In the case at bar, the applicant was in fact denied a hearing because the 2002 school diploma was deemed inadmissible.
holdings.statement: In this case, the applicant was denied a hearing because the 2002 school diploma was deemed inadmissible.

holdings.quote: Further, a restrictive interpretation of this new section would limit the ability of a claimant to get a “full fact-based appeal,” as former Minister of Citizenship and Immigration Jason Kenney intended. I quote his remarks in Hansard (41st Parliament, 1st Session, Tuesday March 6, 2012): “I reiterate that the bill would also create the new refugee appeal division. The vast majority of claimants who are coming from countries that do normally produce refugees would for the first time, if rejected at the refugee protection division, have access to a full fact-based appeal at the refugee appeal division of the IRB. This is the first government to have created a full fact-based appeal.”
holdings.statement: A restrictive interpretation of subsection 110(4) would limit claimants' ability to obtain a full fact-based appeal as intended by the former Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

holdings.quote: Accordingly, in order for there to be a “full fact-based appeal” before the RAD, the criteria for the admissibility of evidence must be sufficiently flexible to ensure it can occur. Often, the evidence at stake will be essential for proving the factual basis of the errors the claimant alleges were made by the RPD. This consideration becomes all the more pertinent in light of the strict timelines a claimant now faces for initially submitting evidence before the RPD. A claimant now has 50 days to present all documents from the date he or she made the claim; the previous legislative scheme required the documents 20 days prior to a hearing, which, on average, took much longer to take place. When the RPD confronts a claimant on the weakness of his evidentiary record, the RAD should, in subsequent review of the decision, have some leeway in order to allow the claimant to respond to the deficiencies raised
holdings.statement: For a full fact-based appeal before the RAD, the admissibility criteria must be flexible to allow essential evidence to prove errors alleged by the claimant, especially given strict timelines for submitting evidence to the RPD.

holdings.quote: But there is more. In Raza, Justice Sharlow distinguishes between the express and the implicit questions raised by paragraph 113(a) of the Act and specifically states that the four implied questions (credibility, relevance, newness and materiality) find their source in the purpose of paragraph 113(a) within the statutory scheme of the Act relating to refugee claims and PRRA applications. In my view, they need to be addressed in that specific context and are not transferable in the context of an appeal before the RAD.
holdings.statement: The Raza test's implied questions (credibility, relevance, newness, materiality) arise from the context of paragraph 113(a) and are not transferable to the RAD appeal context.

holdings.quote: In sum, I am of the view that it was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the Raza test in interpreting subsection 110(4) of the Act all the while failing to appreciate that its role is quite different from that of a PRRA officer.
holdings.statement: It was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the Raza test in interpreting subsection 110(4) without appreciating its different appellate role from a PRRA officer.

holdings.quote: In order to achieve statutory coherence, in that the RAD would be able to hear fleshed out appeals of questions of fact and of mixed fact and law, the main issue is whether the evidence “was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably (or normally according to the French version) have been expected in the circumstances to have presented.”
holdings.statement: The main issue is whether the evidence was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it, under subsection 110(4) of the Act.

holdings.quote: These findings surely affected the totality of the credibility assessment made by the RPD.
holdings.statement: These findings affected the totality of the credibility assessment made by the RPD.

holdings.quote: In my mind, it was unreasonable for the RAD to expect the applicant to file a complaint against his former lawyer as a prerequisite for filing the new evidence before the RAD.
holdings.statement: It was unreasonable for the RAD to expect the applicant to file a complaint against his former lawyer as a prerequisite for filing the new evidence before the RAD.

holdings.quote: It was unreasonable for the RAD to expect the applicant to know of the complaints procedure before the Barreau du Québec, much less be willing to attack the competence and ethics of that lawyer.
holdings.statement: It was unreasonable for the RAD to expect the applicant to know of the complaints procedure before the Barreau du Québec or to be willing to attack the competence and ethics of that lawyer.

holdings.quote: The applicant’s request to file this new evidence fell squarely, in my view, within the scope of subsection 110(4) of the Act and it met its explicit criteria. * * *
holdings.statement: The applicant’s request to file the new evidence fell squarely within the scope of subsection 110(4) of the Act and met its explicit criteria.

holdings.quote: As indicated above, I am of the view that said question is not determinative of the present case and that it would not be determinative of an appeal.
holdings.statement: The question proposed about RAD's deference to RPD findings is not determinative of the present case or an appeal.

holdings.quote: However, I view the following questions as being of general importance and determinative in the case at bar: • What standard of review should be applied by this Court when reviewing the Refugee Appeal Division’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27? • In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board, sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 apply to its subsection 110(4)?
holdings.statement: The following questions are of general importance and determinative in this case: the standard of review for the Court when reviewing RAD's interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA; and whether the test in Raza v Canada for paragraph 113(a) applies to subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: VII. Conclusion [66] For these reasons, I find that both the RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act and its application to the facts before it are unreasonable such that the application for judicial review should be granted and the above questions certified.
holdings.statement: Both the RAD's interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Act and its application to the facts are unreasonable, warranting granting the application for judicial review.

holdings.quote: JUDGMENT THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that: 1. The applicant’s Application for Judicial Review is granted; 2. The decision of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board, dated September 26, 2013, is set aside and the matter is remitted back to a different member for re-determination; 3. The following questions of general importance are certified: • What standard of review should be applied by this Court when reviewing the Refugee Appeal Division’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27? • In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board, sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 apply to its subsection 110(4)?
holdings.statement: The applicant's application for judicial review is granted; the RAD decision dated September 26, 2013 is set aside and remitted to a different member for re-determination; and the two questions of general importance are certified.

authorities.quote: In Alberta Teachers, Justice Binnie set out that an issue of general legal importance is one “whose resolution has significance outside the operation of the statutory scheme under consideration.” The Supreme Court of Canada has since not identified a case that raised a “question of central importance to the legal system as a whole.” Moreover, since Alberta Teachers, the Supreme Court of Canada has reiterated its strict limitations to the use of the exceptions to the reasonableness standard. In McLean v British Columbia (Securities Commission), 2013 SCC 67, the Court found that deference is owed to provincial securities’ regulators interpretation of statute of limitation provisions, despite it being a “technical” question, rather than a “bureaucratic” one.
authorities.authority: Alberta Teachers and subsequent Supreme Court cases limit the use of exceptions to the reasonableness standard, emphasizing deference to tribunal interpretations unless issues are of general legal importance outside the statutory scheme.
